q: A delivery van can safely carry a load of no more than 1.5 tons. Each crate of medical supplies weighs 140 pounds. What is the greatest number of crates the van can carry on one trip?

q: A board is 8 feet 3 inches long. A carpenter cuts off a piece that is 2 feet 7 inches long. Ignoring the width of the saw cut, how long is the remaining piece of board?
w: Borrow 1 foot: 8 ft 3 in = 7 ft 15 in. 7 ft 15 in - 2 ft 7 in = 5 ft 8 in. Check: 99 in - 31 in = 68 in = 5 ft 8 in.

n.1: This borrows 12 inches correctly but does not reduce the 8 feet to 7 feet.
n.2: This borrows 1 foot as 10 inches (13 - 7 = 6); 1 ft = 12 in, so 15 - 7 = 8.
n.3: This subtracts 3 from 7 instead of borrowing a foot from the 8 feet.

q: Brand A oatmeal costs $5.28 for a 1.5-pound canister. Brand B oatmeal costs $4.60 for a 20-ounce canister. Which brand costs less per ounce, and by how much per ounce?
w: 1.5 lb × 16 = 24 oz. Brand A: $5.28 ÷ 24 = $0.22 per oz. Brand B: $4.60 ÷ 20 = $0.23 per oz. Brand A is cheaper by $0.01 per ounce.

n.0: This treats 1.5 lb as 15 oz. Since 1.5 lb = 24 oz, Brand A costs $0.22 per ounce.
n.2: This uses 12 oz per pound (1.5 lb = 18 oz); 1 lb = 16 oz.
n.3: $0.16 is the difference per pound ($3.52 vs. $3.68), not per ounce.

q: A hallway is 42 yards long. Baseboard trim is sold in 8-foot pieces. How many pieces must be bought to run trim along both long sides of the hallway? Assume there are no doorways.
w: 42 yd × 3 = 126 ft per side, so both sides = 252 ft. 252 ÷ 8 = 31.5, so round up to 32 pieces.

q: A recipe for a clinic bake sale calls for 3/4 cup of oil, but the only measure on hand is a tablespoon. How many tablespoons of oil are needed?
w: 1 cup = 8 fl oz and 1 fl oz = 2 tbsp, so 1 cup = 16 tbsp. 3/4 × 16 = 12 tbsp. Check: 12 tbsp ÷ 2 = 6 fl oz = 3/4 of 8 fl oz.

n.0: 36 is the number of teaspoons in 3/4 cup (3/4 × 48); divide by 3 to get tablespoons.
n.1: This counts 1 tablespoon per fluid ounce (3/4 × 8 = 6); 1 fl oz = 2 tbsp.
n.2: This uses 16 fl oz per cup (the pint value), which doubles the answer.

q: A traveler rents a car in Canada, where gasoline costs $1.70 per liter. The car's tank holds 12 gallons. Use 1 gallon = 3.785 liters. How much will it cost to fill the empty tank? Enter the number of dollars, rounded to the nearest dollar.

q: A hospital cafeteria needs 12 gallons of soup for a staff event. The soup comes in 4-liter containers. Use 1 liter = 1.06 quarts. What is the least number of containers the cafeteria must order?
w: 12 gal × 4 = 48 qt. 48 ÷ 1.06 = 45.28 L. 45.28 ÷ 4 = 11.32, so round up to 12 containers.

q: A patient is prescribed 1 tablespoon of cough syrup three times a day for 5 days. The pharmacy needs the total volume in milliliters. How many milliliters of cough syrup will the patient take over the full 5 days?

q: A child's liquid antibiotic dose is 1 1/2 teaspoons twice a day. The bottle holds 4 fluid ounces. Use 1 fluid ounce = 30 milliliters. How many full days will the bottle last at this dose?
w: Dose = 1.5 × 5 mL = 7.5 mL; per day = 2 × 7.5 = 15 mL. Bottle = 4 × 30 = 120 mL. 120 ÷ 15 = 8 days.

q: During one shift, a patient drinks 2 cups of broth, 6 fluid ounces of juice, and 3 tablespoons of a liquid supplement. Use 1 cup = 240 milliliters. What is the total intake? Enter your answer in milliliters.

q: A home oral rehydration recipe calls for 6 level teaspoons of sugar per liter of clean water. A parent is making 1.5 liters of the solution but has a tablespoon measure and no teaspoon. How many tablespoons of sugar are needed?

q: A patient on a fluid restriction may drink 1,800 mL per day. So far today the patient has had 3 cups of coffee and 10 fl oz of water. Use 1 cup = 240 mL. How many more milliliters may the patient drink today?
w: Coffee: 3 × 240 = 720 mL. Water: 10 × 30 = 300 mL. Total so far = 1,020 mL. Remaining = 1,800 - 1,020 = 780 mL.

q: A child takes 1/2 teaspoon of a liquid vitamin three times a day for 10 days. The oral syringe that comes with the bottle is marked in milliliters. How many milliliters of the vitamin will the child take over the 10 days?

q: A patient weighed 187 pounds at admission and 176 pounds at discharge. The chart records weight in kilograms. Use 1 kilogram = 2.2 pounds. How many kilograms did the patient lose during the hospital stay?

q: A patient's height is measured as 5 feet 4 inches, but the electronic record requires height in centimeters. Use 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters. What height should be entered, to the nearest tenth of a centimeter?

q: A newborn weighs 3,400 grams at birth, and the parents ask for the weight in pounds. Use 1 kilogram = 2.2 pounds. What is the newborn's weight in pounds? Enter the number of pounds, rounded to the nearest tenth.

q: A wound measured 7.62 centimeters long at its first assessment. One week later, it was 2 inches shorter. Use 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters. What was the length of the wound, in centimeters, after one week?

q: A hospital shuttle drives between a clinic and the main hospital, a distance of 18 kilometers one way. The shuttle makes 5 round trips each day. Use 1 mile = 1.6 kilometers. How many miles does the shuttle drive each day?

q: A newborn weighed 3.2 kilograms at birth and 3.65 kilograms at a two-week checkup. Use 1 ounce = 28 grams. To the nearest whole ounce, how much weight did the newborn gain?

q: A toddler weighs 13.5 kg at a well-child visit. What is the toddler's weight in pounds, to the nearest tenth?

q: A wound is 6.35 cm long. What is its length in inches?

q: A newborn weighs 3.6 kg. What is the newborn's weight in pounds and ounces, to the nearest ounce?

q: A provider orders 0.375 gram of a medication to be given once daily. The pharmacy stocks the drug as tablets labeled in milligrams. How many milligrams of the drug does the daily order call for?

q: A roll of oxygen tubing is cut into two pieces for a home-care kit. The first piece measures 1.12 meters, and the second piece measures 1,165 millimeters. How many centimeters longer is the second piece than the first?
w: Put both lengths in the same unit first: 1.12 m = 1,120 mm. Difference = 1,165 - 1,120 = 45 mm. Since 10 mm = 1 cm, 45 mm = 4.5 cm. Check in centimeters: 116.5 cm - 112 cm = 4.5 cm.

q: Each tablet of a vitamin supplement contains 0.05 milligram of vitamin B12, and a patient takes 3 tablets a day. The dietitian's log records vitamin doses in micrograms. How many micrograms of vitamin B12 does the patient take each day?

q: A hospital's indoor walking path is 750 meters long. As part of a rehabilitation plan, a patient walks 4 laps of the path each day for 5 days. How many kilometers does the patient walk in total over the 5 days?
w: Total meters = 750 × 4 × 5 = 15,000 m. Meters to kilometers: divide by 1,000, so 15,000 m = 15 km.

q: A child who weighs 18 kilograms is prescribed a medication at 15 milligrams per kilogram per day, divided into 3 equal doses. How many grams of the medication are in each dose? Enter your answer in grams.

q: A lab technician has 2.5 liters of a buffer solution. Each test tube must be filled with exactly 15 milliliters of the solution. How many test tubes can be completely filled from the 2.5 liters?
w: 2.5 L × 1,000 = 2,500 mL. 2,500 ÷ 15 = 166.67. Only complete tubes count, so round down to 166.

q: A wound measured 3.4 centimeters long when it was assessed on Monday. On Friday, the same wound measured 27 millimeters long. By how many millimeters did the length of the wound decrease?

q: A nutrition study records each participant's fluid intake in deciliters. One participant drank 1.8 liters of water during the day. How many deciliters should the researcher record for this participant?

q: Four specimen containers are labeled with their capacities: container W holds 0.45 L, container X holds 405 mL, container Y holds 4.6 dL, and container Z holds 44 cL. Which container has the greatest capacity?
w: Convert to milliliters: W = 0.45 × 1,000 = 450 mL; X = 405 mL; Y = 4.6 × 100 = 460 mL; Z = 44 × 10 = 440 mL. Container Y holds the most.

n.1: 405 is the largest number shown, but 405 mL is less than 450 mL and 460 mL.
n.2: 44 cL = 440 mL, which is less than 460 mL.
n.3: 0.45 L = 450 mL, which is less than 4.6 dL = 460 mL.

q: An IV infusion pump delivers fluid at a constant rate of 125 milliliters per hour. If the rate is not changed, how many liters of fluid will the patient receive during a 12-hour shift?

q: A research protocol lists a vitamin supplement dose as 3 mg, but the lab's analysis software accepts doses in micrograms (mcg). Which value should be entered?

q: A water jug holds 5 gallons. Use 1 gallon = 3.8 liters. How many 500-mL bottles can be filled from the jug?

n.0: This converts 19 L to 190,000 mL (× 10,000) before dividing by 500.
n.1: This treats the 5 gallons as 5 liters (5,000 ÷ 500 = 10).
n.3: This rounds the factor to 4 L per gallon; use the 3.8 L given in the stem.

q: A dose of 0.2 mg is ordered. The vial contains 50 mcg per mL. How many milliliters should be drawn up?
w: Same units first: 0.2 mg × 1,000 = 200 mcg. 200 mcg ÷ 50 mcg/mL = 4 mL.

n.0: This divides 0.2 by 50 without changing milligrams to micrograms.
n.2: This changes 0.2 mg to 20 mcg (× 100) before dividing by 50.
n.3: This changes 0.2 mg to 2,000 mcg (× 10,000) before dividing by 50.

q: A bottle holds 120 mL of vanilla. Each batch of a recipe uses 1 1/2 tablespoons. How many full batches can be made?
w: 1 1/2 tbsp × 15 mL/tbsp = 22.5 mL per batch. 120 ÷ 22.5 = 5.33, so 5 full batches.

n.0: This uses 5 mL per tablespoon (7.5 mL per batch); 5 mL is a teaspoon.
n.1: This uses 30 mL per tablespoon (45 mL per batch); 30 mL is a fluid ounce.
n.3: 120 ÷ 22.5 = 5.33, and the sixth batch would run short, so round down.

q: A bandage roll is 4 yards long. What is its length in centimeters, to the nearest centimeter?
w: 4 yd × 36 in/yd = 144 in. 144 × 2.54 = 365.76, which rounds to 366 cm.

n.0: This divides 144 in by 2.54; inches to centimeters means multiplying.
n.1: This converts 4 yd to 12 ft and then treats the 12 as inches (12 × 2.54).
n.2: This uses 12 inches per yard (48 in × 2.54); 1 yd = 36 in.

q: A solution contains 2 g of a drug in 500 mL. How many milligrams of the drug are in 1 mL?

n.0: This divides 500 by 2, which gives milliliters per gram, not milligrams per milliliter.
n.2: This changes 2 g to 200 mg (× 100) before dividing by 500.
n.3: 0.004 is the amount in grams per mL (2 ÷ 500); it was not changed to milligrams.

q: A patient's oral temperature is recorded as 38.5 °C in the hospital chart. The patient's home thermometer reads in degrees Fahrenheit. What is the patient's temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

n.1: This rounds 38.5 °C up to 39 °C before converting; round only at the end, and (9/5)(38.5) + 32 = 101.3 °F.
n.2: This adds the 1.5 °C gap between 37 °C and 38.5 °C straight onto 98.6 °F. A Celsius degree equals 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees, so the gap is 2.7 °F.
n.3: This multiplies by 2 instead of 9/5 (2 × 38.5 + 32 = 109); the factor is 9/5 = 1.8.

q: A vaccine refrigerator log lists a reading of 41 °F. The clinic's storage policy lists temperature limits in degrees Celsius. What is the refrigerator's temperature in degrees Celsius?

n.1: This subtracts 32 but then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.
n.2: This multiplies 41 by 5/9 without first subtracting 32.
n.3: This multiplies by 5/9 and then subtracts 32; subtract 32 first.

q: A child has a fever of 102.2 °F. The pediatric chart records temperatures in degrees Celsius. What is the child's temperature in degrees Celsius? Round to the nearest tenth if necessary, and enter the number only.

tr.126.4: Subtracted 32 and then multiplied by 9/5 instead of 5/9.

q: Between 8 a.m. and noon, a patient's temperature rose from 37.2 °C to 38.7 °C. The family asks how much the temperature went up in Fahrenheit terms. By how many degrees Fahrenheit did the temperature rise?

n.1: 1.5 is the rise in degrees Celsius; each Celsius degree equals 9/5 Fahrenheit degrees.
n.2: This adds 32 to the change. The 32 shifts the starting point of the scale, so it cancels out of a difference.
n.3: This multiplies the 1.5 °C change by 5/9 instead of 9/5.

q: A clinic thermometer shows a patient's temperature as 100.4 °F. The student nurse charting it needs the value in degrees Celsius. Which value is correct?

n.0: This rounds 5/9 to 0.55 before multiplying (68.4 x 0.55 = 37.6); 5/9 is 0.555..., so round only at the end.
n.1: This divides 68.4 by 2 instead of by 1.8 (dividing by 1.8 is the same as multiplying by 5/9).
n.3: This multiplies by 5/9 first and subtracts 32 afterward (100.4 x 5/9 = 55.8; 55.8 - 32 = 23.8); subtract 32 first.

q: A parent reports that a child's temperature was 104 °F at home. Convert this temperature to degrees Celsius. Enter your answer in degrees Celsius as a whole number.

tr.26: Multiplied by 5/9 first and then subtracted 32 (104 x 5/9 = 57.8; 57.8 - 32 = 25.8).
tr.72: Subtracted 32 but did not multiply by 5/9.

q: An enzyme lab protocol written in Celsius says to keep samples at 30 °C, but the water bath in the lab displays only degrees Fahrenheit. Which setting matches the protocol?

n.0: This multiplies by 9/5 but leaves out adding 32.
n.1: This adds 32 but leaves out multiplying by 9/5.
n.3: This adds 32 first and then multiplies by 5/9, mixing up the two conversion formulas.

q: Convert 35.5 °C to degrees Fahrenheit.

n.0: This multiplies by 9/5 but leaves out adding 32.
n.1: This multiplies by 5/9 (the Fahrenheit-to-Celsius factor) and then adds 32.
n.3: This rounds 35.5 °C up to 36 °C before converting; round only at the end.

q: Convert 99.5 °F to degrees Celsius, to the nearest tenth.

n.1: This rounds 5/9 to 0.55 before multiplying (67.5 × 0.55 = 37.1); 5/9 = 0.555..., so round only at the end.
n.2: This multiplies by 5/9 first and then subtracts 32; subtract 32 first.
n.3: This multiplies 99.5 by 5/9 without subtracting 32.

q: Which temperature reading is the highest?

n.1: 101.3 °F = 38.5 °C, which is below 38.6 °C.

q: An autoclave sterilizes instruments at 121 °C. What is this temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

n.1: This adds 32 before multiplying ((121 + 32) × 1.8 = 275.4).
n.2: This uses the Fahrenheit-to-Celsius formula ((121 - 32) × 5/9 = 49.4).
n.3: This multiplies by 9/5 but leaves out adding 32.

q: A patient's temperature falls from 102.2 °F to 99.5 °F. By how many degrees Celsius did the temperature fall?
w: The fall is 2.7 °F. A change of 1 °F is 5/9 of a Celsius degree, so 2.7 × 5/9 = 1.5 °C. Check: 102.2 °F = 39 °C and 99.5 °F = 37.5 °C; 39 - 37.5 = 1.5.

n.0: This applies the 5/9 factor twice (1.5 × 5/9 = 0.8).
n.1: 2.7 is the fall in Fahrenheit degrees; it still has to be multiplied by 5/9.
n.2: This multiplies the 2.7 °F change by 9/5 instead of 5/9.

q: Convert 50 °F to degrees Celsius.

n.1: This subtracts 32 but then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.
n.2: This multiplies 50 by 5/9 first (27.8) and then subtracts 32.
n.3: This multiplies 50 by 5/9 without subtracting 32.

q: Write 49 in Roman numerals.
w: 49 = 40 + 9 = XL + IX = XLIX. I may be subtracted only from V or X, so 49 is not IL.

n.1: IL is not standard: I is subtracted only from V or X, never from L.
n.3: X may not repeat four times; 40 is written XL.

q: What number does the Roman numeral CDXLVI represent?

n.0: This reads CD as 600; C before D is subtracted, so CD = 400.
n.1: This reads XL as 60; a smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted, so XL = 40.
n.2: This adds every symbol (500 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 6) and subtracts neither pair.

q: Write 2,019 in Roman numerals.
w: 2,000 = MM, 10 = X, 9 = IX. Together: MMXIX.

n.0: Only one smaller symbol may be subtracted at a time, so IIX is not standard; 19 is XIX.
n.1: Symbols run from largest to smallest; IX (9) cannot come before X (10).
n.2: I may not repeat four times; 9 is written IX.

q: What is the value of the Roman numeral MCDXC?

n.0: This reads XC as 110 instead of 100 - 10 = 90.
n.2: This reads both pairs as sums (CD = 600, XC = 110).
n.3: This reads CD as 600 instead of 500 - 100 = 400.

q: Write 94 in Roman numerals.
w: 94 = 90 + 4 = XC + IV = XCIV.

n.0: CXIV = 100 + 10 + 4 = 114; the C must come after the X to mean 90.
n.1: XCVI = 90 + 6 = 96; 4 is IV, not VI.
n.3: X may not repeat four times; 90 is written XC.

q: What is CX minus XLIV, written as a Roman numeral?
w: CX = 110 and XLIV = 44. 110 - 44 = 66 = LXVI.

n.0: This reads IV as 6, so XLIV becomes 46 and 110 - 46 = 64.
n.1: This reads XLIV as 66 by adding every symbol (110 - 66 = 44).
n.3: This reads XL as 60, so XLIV becomes 64 and 110 - 64 = 46.

q: Which Roman numeral is written in standard form?
w: XLV = 40 + 5 = 45, using the standard pair XL.

n.1: V is never subtracted; 45 is written XLV.
n.2: Only one I may be subtracted at a time; 8 is written VIII.
n.3: L never repeats; 100 is written C.

q: A hospital cornerstone is engraved MCMLXIV. In what year was the cornerstone laid?

n.0: This reads IV as 6; I before V is subtracted, so IV = 4.
n.2: This reads CM as 1,100 instead of 1,000 - 100 = 900.
n.3: This reads LX as 40; L before X is added, so LX = 60 (40 is XL).

q: Write 2,048 in Roman numerals.
w: 2,000 = MM, 40 = XL, 8 = VIII. Together: MMXLVIII.

n.1: MMLXVIII = 2,068; LX is 60, and 40 is XL.
n.2: 8 is written VIII; subtracting two I's from X is not standard.
n.3: X may not repeat four times; 40 is written XL.

q: Which Roman numeral has the greatest value?
w: CDXC = 490; CDXCIX = 499; DIX = 509; CCCXCIX = 399. DIX is the greatest.

n.1: CDXCIX = 400 + 90 + 9 = 499; reading CD as 600 makes it look larger than 509.
n.2: CCCXCIX = 300 + 90 + 9 = 399, which is less than 509.
n.3: CDXC = 400 + 90 = 490, which is less than 509.

q: What is IX × VI, written as a Roman numeral?
w: IX = 9 and VI = 6. 9 × 6 = 54 = L + IV = LIV.

n.0: LVI = 50 + 5 + 1 = 56; 4 is written IV, with the I before the V, so 54 is LIV.
n.1: This reads VI as 4 (9 × 4 = 36); VI = 5 + 1 = 6.
n.2: This reads IX as 11 (11 × 6 = 66); I before X is subtracted, so IX = 9.

q: Write 909 in Roman numerals.
w: 900 = CM and 9 = IX. Together: CMIX.

n.0: I may not repeat four times; 9 is written IX.
n.1: CMXI = 900 + 11 = 911; 9 is IX, with the I first.
n.2: C may not repeat four times; 900 is written CM.

q: Which is the standard Roman numeral for 1,999?
w: 1,000 = M, 900 = CM, 90 = XC, 9 = IX. Together: MCMXCIX.

n.0: I may be subtracted only from V or X, never from M.
n.2: C may not repeat four times; 900 is written CM.
n.3: IC for 99 is not standard; I may be subtracted only from V or X, so 99 is XCIX.

q: A medication is given every 6 hours. The first dose was given at 2140 (24-hour clock). At what time is the third dose due, in 12-hour time?
w: Second dose: 2140 + 6 h = 0340. Third dose: 0340 + 6 h = 0940, which is 9:40 a.m. The third dose comes two intervals (12 hours) after the first.

n.0: 3:40 a.m. (0340) is the second dose.
n.2: 3:40 p.m. adds three 6-hour intervals (18 h); the third dose is only two intervals after the first.
n.3: 0940 is before noon, so it is 9:40 a.m.; 9:40 p.m. would be written 2140.

q: A patient's evening medication is due at 7:45 p.m. How is this time written in military time?
w: For 1:00 p.m. to 11:59 p.m., add 12 to the hour: 7 + 12 = 19, so 1945.

n.0: 0745 is 7:45 a.m.; 12 must be added to a p.m. hour.
n.1: This adds 14 to the hour; 2145 is 9:45 p.m.
n.3: This adds 10 to the hour; 1745 is 5:45 p.m.

q: A monitor alarm is logged at 0030. What is this time in standard time?
w: Hour 00 is the midnight hour, so 0030 is 30 minutes after midnight: 12:30 a.m.

n.0: 11:30 p.m. is 2330, half an hour before midnight.
n.1: 12:30 p.m. is 1230, the noon hour.
n.2: 1:30 a.m. is 0130; hour 00 is the 12 a.m. hour.

q: Which pair shows the same time in military and standard form?
w: 0005 is 5 minutes after midnight, which is 12:05 a.m.

n.0: 1305 is 1:05 p.m.; nothing is added to the noon hour, so 12:05 p.m. is 1205.
n.2: 0005 is just after midnight, so it is a.m.; 12:05 p.m. is 1205.
n.3: 1205 is 5 minutes after noon, so it is 12:05 p.m.

q: A blood sample is drawn at 1745. What is this time in standard time?
w: Hours 13 to 23 are p.m.: subtract 12. 17 - 12 = 5, so 5:45 p.m.

n.0: This subtracts 10 instead of 12 (17 - 10 = 7).
n.1: Hours after 12 are p.m., so 1745 cannot be a morning time.
n.2: This subtracts 10 and also labels the time a.m.

q: Which list orders these times from earliest to latest in one day: 0915, 1:30 p.m., 1105, 12:45 a.m.?

n.0: This puts 12:45 a.m. at the end of the day; it is 0045, 45 minutes after midnight.
n.1: This treats 12:45 a.m. as 12:45 p.m. (1245), which would fall after 1105.
n.3: This reads 1:30 p.m. as 0130 and 12:45 a.m. as the end of the day.

q: A clinic closes for lunch at 12:15 p.m. and reopens at 1:20 p.m. Which pair gives these times in military time?
w: The noon hour stays as written: 12:15 p.m. = 1215. For 1:20 p.m., add 12: 1320.

n.0: This writes the noon hour as 00 and does not add 12 to 1:20 p.m.
n.1: 1215 is right, but 1:20 p.m. needs 12 added: 1320, not 0120.
n.2: Nothing is added to the noon hour; 12:15 p.m. is 1215.

q: A unit's quiet hours run from 2200 to 0600. Which time falls within quiet hours?
w: Quiet hours are 10:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. 11:30 p.m. (2330) falls between them.

n.0: 6:15 a.m. is 0615, which is after quiet hours end at 0600.
n.1: 9:45 p.m. is 2145, which is before quiet hours begin at 2200.

q: A patient's breakfast tray arrives at 7:05 a.m. Which entry records this time in military time?
w: Morning hours keep their number with a leading zero: 7:05 a.m. = 0705.

n.1: This adds 10 to the hour; 1705 is 5:05 p.m.
n.2: 0750 is 7:50 a.m.; the minutes are 05, not 50.
n.3: This adds 12 to a morning hour; 1905 is 7:05 p.m.

q: A nurse charted four times. Which entry is converted correctly?
w: 3:20 p.m.: add 12 to the hour, 3 + 12 = 15, so 1520.

n.0: 12:10 a.m. is in the midnight hour, so it is 0010; 1210 is 12:10 p.m.
n.2: 12 is added to p.m. hours only; 6:05 a.m. is 0605.

q: A surgery ends at 1240. What is this time in standard time?
w: 1200 to 1259 is the noon hour, read as written with p.m.: 12:40 p.m.

n.0: 12:40 a.m. is 0040, in the midnight hour.
n.3: This subtracts 12 from the noon hour; 1200 to 1259 is read as 12:xx p.m.

q: Which military time is a quarter past 4 in the afternoon?
w: A quarter past 4 p.m. is 4:15 p.m. Add 12 to the hour: 1615.

n.0: 0415 is 4:15 a.m.; afternoon hours need 12 added.
n.2: This adds 10 to the hour; 1415 is 2:15 p.m.
n.3: 1645 is 4:45 p.m., a quarter to 5; a quarter past is 15 minutes.

q: Which military time falls between 9:30 p.m. and 10:15 p.m.?
w: 9:30 p.m. = 2130 and 10:15 p.m. = 2215. 2145 (9:45 p.m.) falls between them.

n.0: 1015 is 10:15 a.m., a morning time.
n.3: 0945 is 9:45 a.m.; p.m. hours need 12 added.

q: A nurse started her shift at 6:45 a.m. and clocked out at 7:20 p.m. the same day. How long was she at work?
w: From 6:45 a.m. to 6:45 p.m. is 12 hours. From 6:45 p.m. to 7:20 p.m. is 15 + 20 = 35 minutes. Total: 12 h 35 min.

n.0: 11 h 35 min borrows an hour twice; only one hour is borrowed to turn 20 minutes into 80.
n.1: 13 h 25 min subtracts the hours (19 - 6 = 13) and then the smaller minute value from the larger (45 - 20) instead of borrowing an hour.
n.3: 12 h 25 min subtracts 20 from 45 minutes; from :45 to :20 of the next hour is 35 minutes.

q: A nurse begins a 12.5-hour shift at 6:45 p.m. She stays 40 minutes after the shift ends to finish charting. At what time does she leave?
w: 12.5 hours = 12 hours 30 minutes. 6:45 p.m. + 12 hours = 6:45 a.m.; + 30 minutes = 7:15 a.m. (end of shift); + 40 minutes = 7:55 a.m.

n.1: This reads 12.5 hours as 12 hours 50 minutes; 0.5 hour is 30 minutes.
n.2: Twelve and a half hours after 6:45 p.m. is the next morning, so the time is a.m.
n.3: This is when the shift ends; the 40 minutes of charting must be added.

q: An IV infusion is started at 9:40 a.m. and is programmed to run for 2.6 hours without stopping. At what time will the infusion finish?

n.0: This reads 2.6 hours as 260 minutes (4 h 20 min).
n.1: This reads 2.6 hours as 2 hours 6 minutes; 0.6 h = 0.6 × 60 = 36 min.
n.2: This reads 0.6 hour as 60 minutes, as if an hour had 100 minutes.

q: A patient fasted from 2115 until 0730 the next morning. How long was the fast?
w: Time to midnight: 2400 - 2115 = 2 h 45 min. After midnight: 7 h 30 min. Total: 9 h 75 min = 10 h 15 min.

n.0: This turns 75 minutes into 15 minutes but does not carry the extra hour.
n.1: This subtracts 2115 from 2400 like ordinary numbers (285, read as 2 h 85 min = 3 h 25 min).
n.2: This subtracts 0730 from 2115 as if both times were on the same day.

q: An IV infusion started at 1350 and finished at 1625. How long did it run?
w: Borrow 1 hour as 60 minutes: 16 h 25 min = 15 h 85 min. 15 h 85 min - 13 h 50 min = 2 h 35 min.

n.0: This borrows 100 minutes (1625 - 1350 = 275, read as 2 h 75 min = 3 h 15 min).
n.1: This counts 1400 to 1625 (2 h 25 min) and leaves out the 10 minutes from 1350 to 1400.
n.3: This subtracts the smaller minutes from the larger (50 - 25) without borrowing.

q: A dose is given at 2245. The next dose is due 8 hours later. At what military time is it due?
w: 2245 + 8 h = 3045. Past 2400, subtract 24 hours: 3045 - 2400 = 0645 the next morning.

n.0: This subtracts 12 hours from 3045 instead of 24.
n.2: This subtracts 8 hours instead of adding them.
n.3: This does not wrap past midnight; subtract 24 hours from 3045.

q: A tube feeding starts at 1915 and runs for 9 hours 50 minutes. At what military time does it end?
w: 1915 + 9 h 50 min = 28 h 65 min = 29 h 05 min. Subtract 24 hours: 0505 the next morning.

n.0: This does not wrap past midnight; subtract 24 hours from 2905.
n.2: This subtracts 12 hours from 2905 instead of 24.
n.3: This drops 60 of the 65 minutes without carrying 1 hour into the hour count.

q: A procedure that lasts 1.75 hours begins at 1340. At what military time does it end?

n.0: This adds 75 minutes, reading 1.75 hours as 75 minutes.
n.1: This adds 175 minutes, reading 1.75 hours as 175 minutes.
n.3: This reads 1.75 hours as 1 hour 75 minutes.

q: A nurse works from 0645 to 1920 with a 30-minute unpaid break. How much paid time does she work?
w: 1920 - 0645: borrow 1 hour, 18 h 80 min - 6 h 45 min = 12 h 35 min. Minus the 30-minute break: 12 h 5 min.

n.0: This subtracts 20 from 45 without borrowing (13 h 25 min) before taking off the break.
n.1: 12 h 35 min is the whole time at work; the 30-minute break is unpaid.
n.3: This borrows 100 minutes (1920 - 0645 = 1275, read as 13 h 15 min) before taking off the break.

q: A home health visit lasts 105 minutes. The agency bills $40 per hour. What is the charge for the visit?

n.0: This rounds the visit up to 2 hours before billing.
n.1: This writes 1 h 45 min as 1.45 h; 45 minutes is 0.75 hour.
n.2: This reads 105 minutes as 1.05 hours, as if an hour had 100 minutes.

q: A patient fell asleep at 10:50 p.m. and woke at 6:25 a.m. How long did the patient sleep?
w: 10:50 p.m. to midnight is 1 h 10 min. Midnight to 6:25 a.m. is 6 h 25 min. Total: 7 h 35 min.

n.0: This counts from 11:00 p.m. and leaves out the 10 minutes before it.
n.2: This finds 2400 - 2250 = 150 and reads it as 1 h 50 min instead of 1 h 10 min.
n.3: This subtracts 6:25 from 10:50 as if both times were in the same half of the day.

q: A patient may not eat for 8 hours before a procedure at 0730. What is the latest military time the patient may eat?
w: Count back 8 hours from 0730: 7 h 30 min back reaches 0000, and 30 more minutes reaches 2330 the evening before.

n.0: This adds 12 hours instead of 24 before subtracting (1930 - 0800 = 1130).
n.1: This subtracts 7 h 30 min from 8 h and writes the 30-minute difference as a time.
n.3: This adds 8 hours to 0730 instead of counting back.

q: A 3.4-hour infusion starts at 2215. At what military time does it end?
w: 0.4 h × 60 = 24 min, so 3.4 h = 3 h 24 min. 2215 + 3 h 24 min = 2539; subtract 24 hours: 0139.

n.0: This reads 3.4 hours as 3 hours 40 minutes.
n.2: This does not wrap past midnight; subtract 24 hours from 2539.
n.3: This reads 3.4 hours as 3 hours 4 minutes.
